subject: bio
title: Transport and Gas Exchange
subtitle: Integrating gas exchange, blood transport and circulatory adaptations.
concept: CO₂ is transported mainly as hydrogencarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻) in plasma; O₂ is transported mainly by haemoglobin in red blood cells.
The chloride shift maintains electrical neutrality as HCO₃⁻ leaves red blood cells.
Adaptations of red blood cells — biconcave disc shape, no nucleus, packed with Hb — maximise O₂ carrying capacity.

notes.heading: Oxygen Transport
items: 98.5% O₂ is carried as oxyhaemoglobin inside red blood cells; 1.5% dissolved in plasma.
Each haemoglobin molecule carries up to 4 O₂; loading in lungs (high pO₂); unloading in tissues (low pO₂).
Cooperativity: first O₂ binding changes Hb shape → easier for 2nd, 3rd, 4th O₂ to bind → S-shaped dissociation curve.

notes.heading: CO₂ Transport
items: ~70% as HCO₃⁻ in plasma: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ (catalysed by carbonic anhydrase in RBCs). HCO₃⁻ exits RBC into plasma; Cl⁻ enters (chloride shift) to maintain charge balance.
~23% as carbaminohaemoglobin (CO₂ bound to amino groups of Hb).

notes.heading: Red Blood Cell Adaptations
items: Biconcave disc: large surface area : volume ratio for rapid O₂ diffusion; flexible to squeeze through capillaries.
No nucleus: more space for haemoglobin (~280 million Hb per RBC).
No mitochondria: RBCs respire anaerobically → don't use the O₂ they carry.
Short lifespan (~120 days): replaced by new RBCs from bone marrow.

notes.heading: Adaptations in Other Organisms
items: Llamas/alpacas: Hb with higher O₂ affinity at altitude (lower pO₂).
Diving mammals (e.g. seals): higher myoglobin content in muscles; higher blood volume; store O₂ for extended dives.
Insects: use tracheal system; no blood O₂ transport.
Fish: gills; counter-current exchange (covered in gas exchange topic).

definitions.body: The movement of Cl⁻ ions into red blood cells to replace HCO₃⁻ ions that have moved into plasma, maintaining electrical neutrality.
An enzyme in red blood cells that catalyses the reversible reaction CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃.
Haemoglobin with CO₂ bound to its amino groups (~23% of CO₂ transport).
The property of haemoglobin whereby binding of one O₂ molecule increases the affinity for subsequent O₂ molecules, producing an S-shaped dissociation curve.

workedExamples.q: Explain how CO₂ produced by respiring muscle cells is transported to the lungs.

steps.text: CO₂ diffuses from muscle cells into plasma, then into red blood cells.
Inside RBCs, carbonic anhydrase catalyses: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻.
HCO₃⁻ diffuses out of RBCs into plasma; Cl⁻ moves in (chloride shift) to maintain electrical neutrality.
Low CO₂ in alveoli reverses the reaction; CO₂ diffuses into alveoli and is exhaled. H⁺ binds back to Hb.

mistakes: Forgetting that carbonic anhydrase is inside red blood cells (not plasma).
Stating CO₂ is mostly carried dissolved in plasma — 70% is as HCO₃⁻, not dissolved.
Forgetting the chloride shift is needed to maintain electrical neutrality after HCO₃⁻ leaves the RBC.
tips: The Bohr effect links CO₂ transport to O₂ unloading: high CO₂ → low pH → Hb releases O₂ (right shift of curve).
Remember the proportions: ~70% HCO₃⁻, ~23% carbaminoHb, ~7% dissolved.
RBC has no nucleus → more Hb. No mitochondria → doesn't consume O₂ it carries (uses anaerobic respiration).

Catalyses CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ inside red blood cells — speeding up CO₂ transport.

questions.q: What proportion of CO₂ is transported as HCO₃⁻?
questions.exp: About 70% of CO₂ is transported as hydrogencarbonate ions in plasma.

questions.q: Why do red blood cells lack mitochondria?
opts: So they don't consume the O₂ they carry (use anaerobic respiration)
questions.exp: RBCs produce ATP anaerobically — having no mitochondria means the O₂ they carry is available for delivery to tissues.

opts: Cl⁻ entering RBCs as HCO₃⁻ leaves
questions.exp: As HCO₃⁻ leaves RBCs into plasma, Cl⁻ moves in to maintain electrical neutrality — this is the chloride shift.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyses CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ in red blood cells?
questions.exp: Carbonic anhydrase in RBCs dramatically speeds up this reversible reaction.

questions.q: What does the S-shape of the oxygen dissociation curve indicate?
opts: Hb has constant affinity for O₂
Cooperativity — each O₂ bound increases affinity for next
O₂ dissociates in a linear fashion
Hb is fully saturated at all pO₂
questions.exp: Cooperativity causes the S-shape: after the first O₂ binds, affinity increases, so the curve rises steeply, then levels off at saturation.
